For the upper bound we construct a two-stage estimator that uses clipped and binned event data for screening, followed by a least-squares refinement, and apply concentration bounds derived from the Poisson cluster representation. For the lower bound we combine Fano's inequality with Jacod's Girsanov formula for point processes on a suitable subclass of networks.

items.title: Measuring and Decomposing Mode Separation via the Canonical Diffusion
items.description: arXiv:2605.08777v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Mode separation, namely how sharply a distribution fragments into barrier-separated clusters, is a fundamental geometric property of densities, difficult to quantify in high dimensions. Modes are often the meaningful alternatives in the data, such as the conformations of a molecule or the distinct semantic types among a generative model's outputs. Mode separation is distinct from dispersion, which is what standard label-free tools capture: differential entropy rises with spread regardless of fragmentation, and PCA orders directions by variance regardless of barriers. Mutual information does capture it, but only given the latent component labels, which are usually unavailable. We measure mode separation through a single stochastic process intrinsic to the density, namely the unique reversible diffusion with $f$ as its stationary distribution and a constant scalar diffusion coefficient. From its autocovariance matrix we extract two readouts. The first, SSA (Sum of Squared Autocorrelations), is a scalar barrier-sensitive measure. The second, DA (Dominant Autocorrelation directions), gives linear projections ordered by metastability rather than variance. Under an isotropic-Gaussian null, we derive the limiting spectrum of the empirical autocovariance in closed form, generalizing the Marchenko--Pastur law. Its upper edge gives a noise floor that separates metastable directions from sampling noise. Both readouts use only samples and a score function, scaling to high dimensions through pretrained score-based generative models via Tweedie's identity. We apply our framework to three settings: (i) synthetic Gaussian mixtures, where SSA tracks mutual information; (ii) SDXL text-to-image generations, where SSA and DA capture structure that entropy and PCA miss; and (iii) molecular dynamics of alanine dipeptide, where DA recovers the known slow backbone dihedrals from static samples alone.

items.title: Quantum-to-Quantum Transfer Learning Exhibits Improved Robustness in Low-Data Regimes
items.description: arXiv:2605.09118v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Transfer learning under limited data is a challenging setting, where models must adapt to new tasks with minimal supervision. Prior work has primarily focused on improving absolute accuracy in transfer learning. However, empirical evidence comparing quantum and classical models in realistic transfer learning settings remains limited, especially in low-data regimes. In this work, we systematically study the robustness of quantum models under reduced training data. We evaluate multiple quantum and classical architectures across diverse transfer tasks and retraining configurations, and quantify robustness using accuracy degradation and relative performance retention (RPR). Our results show that, although classical models often achieve higher peak performance, they exhibit significantly larger degradation when training data is limited. In contrast, quantum models maintain more stable performance across data regimes, indicating improved robustness and data efficiency. These findings provide empirical evidence that quantum models can offer improved robustness in low-resource transfer learning scenarios.

items.title: Sharp feature-learning transitions and Bayes-optimal neural scaling laws in extensive-width networks
items.description: arXiv:2605.10395v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the information-theoretic limits of learning a one-hidden-layer teacher network with hierarchical features from noisy queries, in the context of knowledge transfer to a smaller student model. We work in the high-dimensional regime where the teacher width $k$ scales linearly with the input dimension $d$ -- a setting that captures large-but-finite-width networks and has only recently become analytically tractable. Using a heuristic leave-one-out decoupling argument, validated numerically throughout, we derive asymptotically sharp characterizations of the Bayes-optimal generalization error and individual feature overlaps via a system of closed fixed-point equations. These equations reveal that feature learnability is governed by a sequence of sharp phase transitions: as data grows, teacher features become recoverable sequentially, each through a discontinuous jump in overlap. This sequential acquisition underlies a precise notion of \textit{effective width} $k_c$ -- the number of learnable features at a given data budget $n$ -- which unifies two distinct scaling regimes: a feature-learning regime in which the Bayes-optimal generalization error $\varepsilon^{\rm BO}$ scales as $ n^{1/(2\beta)-1}$, and a refinement regime in which it scales as $n^{-1}$, where $\beta>1/2$ is the exponent of the power-law feature hierarchy. Both laws collapse to the single relation $\varepsilon^{\rm BO}=\Theta(k_c d/n)$. We further show empirically that a student trained with \textsc{Adam} near the effective width $k_c$ achieves these optimal scaling laws (up to a small algorithmic gap), and provide an information-theoretic account of the associated scaling in model size.

items.title: Quantifying Concentration Phenomena of Mean-Field Transformers in the Low-Temperature Regime
items.description: arXiv:2605.10931v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Transformers with self-attention modules as their core components have become an integral architecture in modern large language and foundation models. In this paper, we study the evolution of tokens in deep encoder-only transformers at inference time which is described in the large-token limit by a mean-field continuity equation. Leveraging ideas from the convergence analysis of interacting multi-particle systems, with particles corresponding to tokens, we prove that the token distribution rapidly concentrates onto the push-forward of the initial distribution under a projection map induced by the key, query, and value matrices, and remains metastable for moderate times. Specifically, we show that the Wasserstein distance of the two distributions scales like $\sqrt{{\log(\beta+1)}/{\beta}}\exp(Ct)+\exp(-ct)$ in terms of the temperature parameter $\beta^{-1}\to 0$ and inference time $t\geq 0$. For the proof, we establish Lyapunov-type estimates for the zero-temperature equation, identify its limit as $t\to\infty$, and employ a stability estimate in Wasserstein space together with a quantitative Laplace principle to couple the two equations. Our result implies that for time scales of order $\log\beta$, which correspond to the early-phase behavior most relevant for practical finite-depth models, the token distribution concentrates at the identified limiting distribution. Numerical experiments confirm this and, beyond that, complement our theory by showing that for finite $\beta$ and large $t$ the dynamics enter a different terminal phase, dominated by the spectrum of the value matrix.

items.title: Kernel-based guarantees for nonlinear parametric models in Bayesian optimization
items.description: arXiv:2605.13160v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern Bayesian optimization and adaptive sampling methods increasingly rely on nonlinear parametric models, such as neural networks, yet theoretical guarantees for such models under adaptive data collection remain limited. Existing analyses largely focus on Gaussian processes, kernel machines, linear models, or linearized neural approximations, leaving a gap between theory and the nonlinear models used in practice. We develop a kernel-based framework for analyzing regularized parametric models trained on adaptively collected data. Our approach uses kernels over the parameter space to induce reproducing kernel Hilbert space structures over the corresponding model class, yielding confidence bounds for models trained with a broad class of regularized losses. We show how these bounds can establish convergence guarantees for approximate Thompson sampling and provide a foundation for analyzing broader likelihood-free Bayesian optimization methods. These results provide a unified route to analyzing nonlinear models in Bayesian optimization and related adaptive optimization settings.

items.title: Batched Stochastic Linear Bandits with 1-Bit Communication Constraints
items.description: arXiv:2605.30976v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study stochastic linear bandits under a natural combination of batching and communication constraints: the time horizon is partitioned into batches of equal size $B$, and during each batch the learner sends $B$ requested arm pulls to an agent, who then observes the corresponding $B$ rewards and responds with a single bit of feedback to the learner. For each batch, the learner specifies the 1-bit quantization rule the agent uses, which may depend on all previously received bits but not on any past rewards directly. This setting addresses a significant yet unexplored ``middle ground'' between previous models having per-round quantization only or total bit budgets only. We establish a minimax lower bound showing that $\Omega(B\min\{d,\log\lvert \mathcal{A} \rvert\})$ regret is unavoidable due to the 1-bit communication bottleneck, even in the absence of noise. Combined with standard statistical limits, this yields a general lower bound of $\widetilde{\Omega}(B\min\{d,\log\lvert \mathcal{A} \rvert\} + \sqrt{dT \min\{d,\log\lvert \mathcal{A} \rvert\}})$. We develop two phased-elimination algorithms based on $G$-optimal designs and 1-bit mean estimation. The first achieves $\widetilde{O}(dB + d\sqrt{T})$ regret, matching the lower bound up to logarithmic factors when $\lvert \mathcal{A} \rvert = \exp(\Omega(d))$, and the second incorporates a safe-arm identification and warm-start procedure to obtain $\widetilde{O}(B\log\lvert \mathcal{A} \rvert + d^{3/2}\sqrt{B} + \sqrt{dT\log\lvert \mathcal{A} \rvert})$ regret, which is near-optimal in broad scaling regimes of $(\lvert \mathcal{A} \rvert, B, d, T)$. Together, our results demonstrate that a single bit of feedback per batch suffices to nearly match the minimax regret of unconstrained linear bandits in broad scaling regimes, even for batch sizes as large as $\Theta(\sqrt{T})$.

items.title: Bidirectional Random Projections
items.description: arXiv:2606.10377v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper analyzes bidirectional random projections for ordinary least squares (OLS) regression under the fixed design setting. Let $(X, Y) \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times p}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be a sample and $W \in \mathbb{R}^{n_1\times n}$, $R \in \mathbb{R}^{p\times p_1}$ be two random projections. We develop an expected excess loss bound for the OLS estimator built on $(WXR, WY)$, extending an established bound for the OLS estimator built on $(XR, Y)$. Our analysis shows that our bound is larger and the gap between the two bounds decays at a rate of approximately $O(1/n_1)$. These findings are confirmed by numerical results.

items.title: MAGIC-SSCIL: Manifold Anchoring and Geometric Incremental Calibration for Semi-Supervised Class Incremental Learning
items.description: arXiv:2608.07586v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Exemplar-free semi-supervised class-incremental learning (SSCIL) asks a model to learn new classes from a few labeled and many unlabeled images without storing past data. A common recipe replays old classes from stored Gaussian statistics and pseudo-labels unlabeled data with a confidence threshold. With one or two labels per class, however, the model's confidence is a poor guide to which pseudo-labels are right, so the statistics that replay depends on rest on few or noisy samples. We propose MAGIC (Manifold Anchoring and Geometric Incremental Calibration), which propagates labels over a k-nearest-neighbor graph of frozen features and uses the propagated confidences as weights in the unlabeled loss and, through Soft-Weighted Geometry Calibration (SWGC), in the class statistics from which phantom features replay old classes. With a frozen ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100, CUB-200, and ImageNet-R at 1%, 5%, and 10% labels, we compare MAGIC with nine supervised class-incremental methods equipped with FixMatch and two native SSCIL methods. MAGIC gains from unlabeled data in all nine settings, most at 1%, and leads on fine-grained CUB-200 at every ratio; at 1% it is level with the best on ImageNet-R and 2.2 points behind the native SSCIL method TACLE on CIFAR-100. Experiments inside MAGIC show that most of this gain flows through the weighted statistics, not the loss, that at 1% labels graph pseudo-labels are more accurate than the model's own at equal coverage, and that a fixed threshold of 0.95 removes most of the gain. At higher ratios, baselines that adapt the backbone or model full covariances overtake MAGIC on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-R.

items.title: Probing and steering biology across Boltz-1s trunk-diffusion boundary
items.description: arXiv:2608.11475v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AlphaFold3-class structure predictors pair a representational trunk, which processes sequence and context, with a diffusion module, which generates atomic coordinates. How biological information changes as it crosses this architectural boundary remains poorly understood. We analyze per-residue activations from the Pairformer trunk and diffusion module of Boltz-1 using linear probes, sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and causal interventions. From the trunk, both geometry (secondary structure, disorder) and sequence chemistry (amino-acid identity, signal peptides, disulfide-bond annotations) are linearly decodable. In the diffusion module, the two diverge. Secondary structure remains equally decodable, whereas sequence chemistry becomes much less linearly accessible. We then test whether decodable directions can steer the model by editing the trunk's single representation. Helix and coil directions change predicted structure dose-dependently, but a beta-strand direction that is highly predictive on the same proteins (held-out F1 =0.78) produces no measurable increase in strand content at any of the steered layers. Removing helix or coil directions does not remove that structure. Linear decodability therefore did not imply causal influence at the sites we tested. The same probes also score markedly lower against SwissProt annotations than against DSSP labels, because unannotated residues that the model gets right are charged as false positives; such scores are therefore lower bounds. Finally, supervised probes outscore single SAE features wherever a label already exists.

items.title: On the Feasibility of Image-Based Representations for Air Traffic Complexity Estimation
items.description: arXiv:2608.11810v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Air traffic controllers perceive traffic complexity through the radar display, suggesting that a computer vision model operating on the same imagery may provide a natural architecture for modeling controller-perceived complexity; however, whether radar imagery is a viable input format for deep learning vision models remains unclear. Unlike natural images, radar images are extremely sparse and self-similar, consisting primarily of a black background and a few visually identical aircraft blobs, while small changes in aircraft positions can substantially alter sector-level complexity. To test whether a vision model can capture these operationally important differences, we encode each traffic situation as a position image supplemented by five channels representing aircraft state variables, including heading, speed, and altitude, and train a Vision Transformer (ViT) to regress four intrinsic complexity components derived from pairwise geometric relations among aircraft. The model achieves $R^2 > 0.96$ for all four components on test data, and a one-aircraft removal perturbation study shows that the change in the model's estimate is proportional to how much the removed aircraft contributed to sector complexity, rather than the same for every removal. These results demonstrate that, despite its atypical visual characteristics, the proposed image-based representation is a viable input format for air traffic complexity modeling.

items.title: Evaluation Resolution Confounds Learning-Rule Comparisons in Model-Brain RSA of Early Visual Cortex
items.description: arXiv:2608.12408v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Revision note: see Comments. Studies of biologically plausible learning rules (feedback alignment, predictive coding, STDP) train small networks on $32\times32$ images and compare them with brain responses to naturalistic stimuli presented at much higher resolution. We find that a common result in this setting, that untrained or locally trained networks rival or beat backpropagation at early visual cortex, depends on the resolution at which networks are evaluated. In representational similarity analysis (RSA) against human V1, the gap between an untrained and a backprop-trained network grows monotonically from $-0.001$ (95% CI $[-0.011, 0.009]$) at the 32 px training resolution to $+0.030$ $[0.018, 0.042]$ at 224 px (six resolutions, 5 seeds; per-subject RSA on cross-run stimulus pairs). The growth reproduces for three further learning rules, directionally in single-seed macaque electrophysiology, along training, and for an ImageNet ResNet-50 and a Swin-Tiny transformer, which also align best at low resolution although trained at 224 px. Gabor and pixel structure, the normalization state of the untrained baseline, and a global brightness statistic do not account for it. Against a criterion fixed before the analysis, limiting image content to 32 px while the input still grows does not shrink the V1 gap ($+0.035$ $[0.023, 0.046]$ vs. $+0.030$ at 224 px; ratio 1.14 $[1.03, 1.34]$): it arises once the input exceeds the training resolution, through a decline of backprop. A single luminance value per image reaches rho= 0.054 against V1, matching the untrained network (0.053), which bounds what RSA on globally pooled features can resolve at V1 in this dataset. The one learning effect that holds across resolution is backprop above untrained at LOC. Comparisons of learning rules or architectures at early visual cortex need to control, and report, the evaluation resolution.

items.title: Graph neural networks and the energetic cavity method for combinatorial optimization
items.description: arXiv:2609.07456v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the use of graph neural networks (GNNs) for finding approximate ground states of Ising models. Efficiently finding these ground states is of broad significance because many combinatorial optimization problems can be formulated as an Ising model with the appropriate choice of couplings and fields. Exactly solving these problems is hard but there are many good heuristic methods. A lineage of these heuristics build from mean-field approximations: one approach uses the leading eigenvector of an appropriately defined matrix, another is the min-sum algorithm, also known as the energetic cavity method. Without modification, GNNs perform worse than both of these methods. We consider small modifications to the GNN to incorporate these heuristics and find that this considerably improves performance. While the modified approach is much stronger than other deep learning approaches, we still find that simulated annealing is generally as good for the same computational cost.

items.title: Fixed Sets and the Hardness of Computing Correlated Equilibria
items.description: arXiv:2610.28141v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We show that computing an approximate correlated equilibrium of a polytope game is PPAD-complete, and thus polynomial-time equivalent to finding a Nash equilibrium. This challenges the conventional view in game theory that correlated equilibria are more tractable objects than Nash equilibria. From a conceptual standpoint, we connect correlated equilibria to a natural generalization of fixed points, which we call fixed sets. A fixed set of a continuous function $f$ is a nonempty finite set $S$ such that $S \subseteq \operatorname{conv} f(S)$. Our main technical contribution is to prove that computing a fixed set is PPAD-hard even at inverse polynomial precision.

items.title: Not All Mislabels Are Equal: Efficient Task-Aware Auditing with Confidence Sequences
items.description: arXiv:2610.33262v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study efficient, adaptive auditing of categorical labels in a fixed dataset, motivated by biodiversity credit programs in which expert verification of species records is costly and downstream scores (e.g., payment) are more sensitive to errors on certain labels than on others. Our proposed ATLAS framework couples anytime-valid inference with a task-aware adaptive auditing policy. Representing label corrections through a confusion matrix, we prioritize which data points to inspect next based on both label uncertainty and the influence of potential label corrections on the downstream score function. In our main case study on Kenyan biodiversity data, task-aware auditing reduces the expert review needed to estimate both the mislabel rate and the nonlinear biodiversity score while maintaining anytime-valid guarantees. We also evaluate ATLAS on public datasets for image classification and named-entity recognition. Across our experiments with linear and nonlinear scores, ATLAS generally reaches the same precision as competing anytime-valid methods with substantially fewer audits. When distribution-free guarantees are prohibitively costly, we develop a model-based Bayesian alternative that can further reduce the number of audits by relying on modeling assumptions. Our biodiversity case study highlights a gap between statistical validity and practical feasibility: generic methods such as Serfling's bound and existing confidence-sequence procedures are rigorous but can require prohibitively many expert reviews in practice. Together, these results show task-aware auditing can significantly reduce the number of expert audits needed while providing finite-sample, anytime-valid guarantees

items.title: Formalizing the Intrinsic Dimension of Objective Landscapes by a Generalized Notion of Co-dimension
items.description: arXiv:2610.39674v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this work, we formalize the concept of intrinsic dimension of objective landscapes introduced in Li et al. (2018), which measures the structural complexity of learning problems by training along randomly generated subspaces. We define the intrinsic dimension of a set $\Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^p$ as the minimal dimension $d_{\mathrm{int}}(\Theta)$ such that a random plane of dimension $d_{\mathrm{int}}(\Theta)$ in $\mathbb{R}^p$ intersects $\Theta$ with probability one. We show that it is a generalized notion of co-dimension that depends on the global geometry of $\Theta$. We study mathematical properties of the intrinsic dimension and develop techniques to estimate the intrinsic dimension of sets $\Theta$ that arise in learning problems. More specifically, we derive upper and/or lower bounds where $\Theta$ is the set of optimal parameters in student-teacher settings with shallow and deep ReLU networks, including finite and infinite sample cases, and with and without regularization. We discuss how our theory leads to novel types of generalization bounds, thereby showing that the intrinsic dimension is a measure of learning complexity. Our results connect techniques from seemingly different areas of machine learning research such as classification of symmetries of ReLU networks and stochastic geometry.

items.title: Sampling Design and Confidence Tubes for Integral Curves on Riemannian Manifolds
items.description: arXiv:2611.00771v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We estimate the integral curve of an unknown vector field from noisy tangent vector field on a known compact Riemannian manifold. We consider two sampling settings: independent observations at random locations that have already been collected, and a fixed response budget that allows subsequent locations to be chosen using pilot information. Under suitable regularity assumptions, the passive kernel estimator has curve error of order $n^{-2/(d+3)}$ in probability, with sample size $n$ and manifold dimension $d$. Its functional central limit theorem has a limit characterized by a linear stochastic differential equation. For active sampling, an independent pilot directs one new batch of measurements to neighborhoods of the target curve. Under localization, smoothness and design conditions, this concentration yields expected maximum curve error of order $N^{-1/2}$, including the pilot in the total response budget $N$. Both methods provide simultaneous geodesic confidence tubes with asymptotically exact coverage under mild conditions. Simulations show narrower active tubes in most reported settings, with improved small-sample coverage in some three-dimensional examples. Ocean-drifter observations illustrate mean-flow reconstruction on the sphere, and a canopy-flow LDA application uses retrospective active sampling to quantify lateral and vertical departures of local mean streamlines.

items.title: What Can a VLA Learn from the Agent That Calls It? Task-Level Experience Distillation for Embodied Navigation
items.description: arXiv:2611.16246v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models drive the robot directly from camera views, yet a VLA alone shows three typical failures. It walks past the goal, stops before reaching it, and rarely recovers after going off track. Pairing a VLA with a large language model (LLM) planner fixes these failures, but queries the LLM throughout every episode, adding token costs and latency. We introduce Harness-to-Executor (H2E), a task-level distillation method that pairs an LLM planner and a frozen VLA as a heterogeneous training agent, keeps only sessions that reach the goal, and then trains a VLA alone on them so no LLM is used at test time. In these sessions, the planner gives sub-instructions and moves the robot with its own tools, detours are common, and the planner decides when to stop. H2E therefore labels every motion as a VLA action for the original task, whoever made it. It masks the loss on steps moving away from the goal and assigns end labels to states near it, so the VLA learns where the task ends. H2E sets a new state of the art on REVERIE-CE and NavRAG-CE. It raises an 8B VLA's success rate by 15.6% and 11.1% respectively, surpassing a method trained on 10M samples. The distilled VLA exceeds its agent on unseen episodes with zero LLM tokens and runs 3.7 times faster.

items.title: Copilot is "the new OS for work," and now Office runs inside of it
items.description: Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the company's vision for its new "frontier ecosystem," announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as "the new OS for work." The announcement is a striking inversion of how we've traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent's work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications. items.title: Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference
items.description: Serving large language models (LLMs) efficiently requires sufficient GPU memory and careful coordination of prompt processing and token generation. GLM-5.3’s FP8 weights, for example, exceed the 640 GB of GPU memory on a single ml.p5.48xlarge instance, before accounting for KV cache and runtime overhead. Long prompts can also slow token generation when both share the same GPUs. Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference now supports NVIDIA Dynamo , combining Dynamo’s distributed inference capabilities with the infrastructure management of HyperPod to address these challenges. Dynamo is an open source distributed inference framework that supports multi-node deployment, disaggregated prefill and decode, and KV-aware routing with engines such as vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM. HyperPod supports these deployments with high-performance Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking, coordinated GPU scheduling, and node health monitoring and recovery. In this post, we illustrate multi-node and disaggregated serving through a deployment example, share benchmark results, and outline best practices for optimizing inference on HyperPod. How the integration works The HyperPod Inference add-on installs the Dynamo custom resource definitions and these serving and scheduling components: HyperPod Inference Operator manages endpoint deployment through an InferenceEndpointConfig (IEC) custom resource. Its dynamoSpec section supplies the Dynamo configuration. Dynamo operator manages resources defined in a DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD) , including the frontend, model workers, replica counts, and resource requirements. Grove coordinates related groups of pods, including multi-node workers, and their scaling relationships. Kubernetes AI (KAI) Scheduler places pods on GPU resources, using gang scheduling to schedule the pods required for a multi-node worker together. AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) provide the Dynamo runtime, while the add-on manages integrated component versions. To adopt a supported Dynamo release, update the add-on. Deployment architecture The following diagram shows the deployment paths, serving components, and infrastructure management for disaggregated inference on SageMaker HyperPod. The Dynamo frontend routes requests to prefill workers, which process prompts, and decode workers, which generate tokens. These separate pools allow independent scaling and tuning. Both pools load the full model weights, and KV cache transfers between them over EFA. Dynamo also supports aggregated serving, where prefill and decode run in the same worker. In either topology, workers can run on one instance or span multiple instances using tensor and pipeline parallelism. Dynamo’s KV-aware router considers reusable prefix KV cache and active worker load in both topologies. Prefix reuse can reduce prompt recomputation and improve time to first token, while load awareness helps avoid overloading workers. For more details on the Dynamo architecture, see the Dynamo Knowledge Base overview . HyperPod provides node, GPU, and EFA health monitoring and manages node replacement, while the orchestration components recreate affected workers. Deployments configured through InferenceEndpointConfig with dynamoSpec support invocation through SageMaker endpoints. Figure 1: Deployment paths, serving components, and infrastructure management for NVIDIA Dynamo on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Two ways to configure your deployment Whether you are new to HyperPod, new to Dynamo, or both, the add-on offers two deployment paths to fit your workflow: Bring-your-own DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD) lets existing Dynamo users continue using upstream documentation, recipes, and manifests, with the Dynamo operator managing the deployment. To bring an existing DGD to HyperPod, use a supported container image and configure storage, networking, and pod placement for your cluster. InferenceEndpointConfig with dynamoSpec lets existing HyperPod Inference users deploy a new Dynamo endpoint using the same configuration format and OpenAI-compatible interface they already know. For the inference engine, you can choose vLLM, SGLang, or TensorRT-LLM, with vLLM used by default. The operator also supplies defaults for KV-aware routing and replica counts. Both paths support single-instance and multi-node deployments. In either case, HyperPod manages node health and replacement. The table summarizes the responsibilities for each path. Dynamo-specific settings belong under spec.dynamoSpec . Model source and endpoint settings are included in the complete manifest. Multi-node aggregated serving This configuration runs one model-worker replica across two instances (16 GPUs), with two frontend replicas for request handling. items.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
items.description: External sandboxes for coding agents I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant , the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects . My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly. external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance. external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package! Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code. The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running: I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches. items.title: Reducing token costs and latency in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore JSON workloads
items.description: As enterprises build production agents with dozens of tools and large structured inputs, token consumption and latency become the primary blockers to a good user experience. When these agents process large JSON data, every additional tool invocation injects the full payload into the large language model (LLM) context window, causing token usage and response latency to spike. Over multi-turn conversations, this pressure compounds, driving up costs and degrading response quality. Effectively managing context-window pressure in agentic systems is key to reliability and responsiveness at scale. In this post, we share three composable strategies we used to build a production agent for Flightscape that handles 20 MB+ JSON payloads. You can apply them to reduce token costs, lower latency, and maintain full reasoning capability across extended sessions. Together, these optimizations reduced token consumption by up to 71% and cut average latency by up to 80% across our benchmark runs on a representative 23 MB payload. Solution overview Flightscape is an airline operations platform that helps airlines plan and manage their crews, flights, and operations. As part of Flightscape’s crew management capabilities, we built a Training Schedule Optimization agent that verifies crew training schedule assignments against business rules. With 40+ tools and JSON inputs in megabytes, this agent could answer complex queries across crew assignments, scheduling, and resource allocation. Although the agent delivered the required functionality, average request latencies exceeded 15 seconds across most calls. Every tool call injected its full payload into the model context, inflating token counts and costs. On larger datasets, the context window filled up before the agent could finish reasoning. The following diagram (Figure 1) details the agentic architecture and data flow: Figure 1: Agent architecture and data flow In Figure 1, the Optimizer receives a Request JSON and produces a Response JSON, which is then validated by a Business Rules Validator to generate a Validation Report JSON. All three JSON documents are ingested by an AI Agent that provides a conversational interface for users to query optimization results, understand validation errors, and explore scheduling assignments. The agent is built with LangGraph , an open source framework by LangChain, and runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can be applied to validate and filter the agent’s conversational responses, helping facilitate responsible AI practices in production deployments. We defined a custom agent state that holds the data needed by our tools: optimization request JSON, optimization response JSON, and validation report JSON. We also added basic statistics and cache data to state for rich queries. The agent uses an Amazon Bedrock model for reasoning and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to persist chat interactions across turns, and each turn follows this flow (Figure 2): Figure 2: Agentic flow This is what the state structure looks like. The state references TOPT (Training Optimizer) request and response objects, which represent the crew scheduling inputs and optimization results: class GraphState(TypedDict): """LangGraph state that combines messages with application data.""" # Messages from conversation (managed by add_messages reducer) messages: Annotated[List[BaseMessage], add_messages] # Application-specific state - parsed domain objects request: Optional[TOPTRequest] responses: List[TOPTResponse] validation_report: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] basic_stats: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] cache_data: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] Note: This state originally held heavy payloads inline. Later sections explain how we moved large artifacts out of conversational context to reduce token usage. We implemented three strategies to reduce the token costs, latency, and memory overhead caused by passing large JSON payloads through the model context. The following diagram (Figure 3) shows how the three strategies fit into a single agent turn. Strategy 1 runs at the start and end of each turn, and Strategies 2 and 3 run each time a tool returns a result. Figure 3: Overview of the three optimization strategies in one agent turn At the start of a turn, the hydrate_state() function restores lightweight session state from AgentCore memory. When a tool returns an oversized list or dictionary, the agent stores the full result in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and passes the model a compact summary with a handle. The model can then retrieve more detail with get_result_page_tool() . At the end of the turn, the dehydrate_state() function writes heavy payloads to the S3ArtifactStore and saves only references to AgentCore memory. The following sections describe each strategy in detail. Prerequisites To implement these strategies, make sure the following are in place: An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock and a supported model. An Amazon S3 bucket for artifact storage. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory enabled for session-state persistence. A LangGraph-based agent (or equivalent graph-orchestration framework) with tool-calling support. A Python 3.12+ environment with boto3 , langchain-core , and langgraph . Optimization strategies The companion code is available in this GitHub repository . Strategy 1: Persist lightweight session state, offload heavy artifacts Our first optimization was to change how we persist session state. Initially, large payloads were being stored too close to the conversational state. We therefore moved heavy artifacts (request JSON, response JSON, validation data, and other large derived payloads) to Amazon S3. AgentCore memory then persists only stable references to these objects, keeping the session state lightweight. To support this, we introduced a dedicated p

items.description: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol OpenAI: We’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work. They're available in the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol . I shipped LLM 0.38 with support for the new models. 6.2 Astra is 80% of the price of 6 Astra - $8/MTok input and $40/MTok output, the same price as Claude Fable 5.2 (which was also 80% of its predecessor). 6 Astra and Fable 5 were both $10/$50. The cached price is an even bigger discount - $0.40/million compared to $1/million for the older model. This is great news for longer running agentic sessions. GPT-6.2 Sol is the same $2/$10 price as 6.1 Sol and 6 Sol - which are half the price of GPT-5.6 Sol ($4/$20). Here are the pelicans for GPT-6.2 Sol and for GPT-6.2 Astra . The 6.2 Astra max pelican looks like this: I have a full comparison grid here , but here's how the high/xhigh/max pelicans compare with the previous Sol and Astra releases: I also ran my most recent benchmark prompt against the two models, using "Ultra' effort levels in the Codex CLI: Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data Here's Sol and here's Astra . Neither of them did a good enough job of morphing Yonkers into a big mech, at least in comparison to Claude Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Carbon . This video showing the Astra and Sol animations playing out at the same time: I created that video using GPT-6.2 Astra (Ultra) in the Codex desktop app by prompting: https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-astra-ultra/index.html and https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-sol-ultra/index.html are two videos of the same thing by two different models I need a video of the first 10 seconds where the top half of the video plays the first and the bottom half plays the second I need an overlaid label of "GPT-6.2 Astra" on the top half and "GPT-6.2 Sol" on the bottom half. These labels should be tastefully positioned. Make the video square and 2000x2000 pixels Then later: OK make it 20s Here's the exported transcript . The buzz around these new models is mixed at the moment. Astra 6.2 isn't scoring quite as high as Fable 5.2 on various benchmarks, and I've seen a few complaints that its communication style can be confusing. Theo Browne's review (in the form of a feedback letter he sent OpenAI during pre-release) has this useful example: When this model is working on long tasks, it can pull in a lot of subagents and manage them pretty well. It will then proceed to randomly ask you some weird internal implementation detail bullshit that you could not under any earthly circumstance understand, much less have input on . I sent "/goal make a new level for Outer Wilds". 2 hours in, it's "blocked" because it wanted to ask me "does r24's reviewer write it's clips to 24_g521.mp4 or 24_p11.mp4?" items.title: Cut generative AI costs: Code for rules, models for judgment
items.description: The biggest cost lever in a generative AI system is whether you call a model at all. We often see teams route every task through a large language model (LLM), including input validation, formatting, and routing. Each call is cheap in isolation, but at production scale these small costs become one of the largest line items in the architecture. Wherever a deterministic rule can do the job, skipping the model saves money, cuts latency, and removes a source of non-determinism. In this post, you learn how to decide whether each step in a workflow needs a model at all. You can then map each option to AWS: deterministic code, a constrained decision call, or a right-sized model on Amazon Bedrock . Why unneeded model calls add up The pattern usually starts in a prototype. A model call works for one step, so it becomes the default for the next. Those steps include validating input, reformatting a request body, and picking a route. At prototype volume, nobody notices the cost. At production volume, unneeded model calls cost you in three ways: Spend grows with request count, even for low-value steps. Latency stacks, because every model call in a chain adds hundreds of milliseconds. Output can vary, because the same input can return a different answer. That makes testing harder and audits slower. Each new model launch then restarts the debate about which model to use. The earlier question, whether the step needs a model at all, goes unasked. Cost guidance, including the AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens , often starts at model selection. This post starts one step earlier: Does the step need a model at all? How to decide whether a step needs a model Figure 1 shows the whole decision as a flowchart with three labeled lanes: Runs as code, Questions, and Runs on a model. Take each workflow step through three questions in order, and stop at the first option that meets the step’s requirements: Can a rule check success, such as a format, a schema, a keyword, or a range? If a rule settles only part of the step, a fast path runs the rule first. Can a model write the rule once, such as a regular expression or a JSON schema? Does the step pick one answer from a fixed list, such as a route, a class, or yes or no? If the answer to all three is no, the step is open-ended and runs on a right-sized model. Figure 1: Deciding whether a workflow step needs a model, and which one Consider a customer support assistant. The following table shows how five of its steps go through the chart. # Step Path through the chart Where it runs 1 Check an order number’s format A rule can check success. Amazon API Gateway REST API request validation, or an AWS Lambda function 2 Route a message by intent A rule settles part of it. A keyword match on the fast path resolves messages such as “refund”, and the residual goes to the third question. An AWS Step Functions Choice state that uses JSONata. The residual goes to a constrained decision call. 3 Extract a tracking number from a carrier email A model can write the rule once. It drafts a regular expression, and you review and commit it. Code, as a committed pattern in AWS Lambda 4 Pick one of four support queues for a ticket The answer comes from a fixed list. A constrained decision call. Unsure answers escalate to the right-sized model. 5 Draft a reply to the customer The task is open-ended. The right-sized model, the smallest Amazon Bedrock model that meets the requirements You can use a model when a task is open-ended, ambiguous, or generative: summarizing a document, drafting a reply, extracting meaning from prose. Use deterministic code when the task has a checkable rule: an email format, a schema, an exact keyword, a numeric range. The following table shows what you trade away when you send a rule-shaped task to a model. Property Deterministic code Model call Cost per invocation Typically orders of magnitude lower Per-token, non-trivial at scale Latency Single-digit milliseconds or less Hundreds of milliseconds Correctness on a well-specified rule Exact for the rule as written High, but with a non-zero error rate Auditability The rule sits in source control Harder to explain to an auditor Behavior over time Stable until you change it Changes when you move to a new model version, or when a version is retired A model can also hallucinate and return different answers to the same input. A temperature of 0 makes varied answers less likely, but it doesn’t guarantee identical output. Amazon Bedrock model evaluation and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails help you measure and contain these risks. A rule has neither problem, which is one reason regulated workloads favor rules. A useful test: If you can write the acceptance test as a rule, you can usually write the step as a rule. For more information, refer to Orchestration models: From rule-based to AI-native in AWS Prescriptive Guidance. Decide, don’t generate Most routing and classification steps sit between a rule and open-ended generation. A rule can’t decide every case, but these steps don’t need generated text either. They need one answer from a fixed list of options that you define in advance, like the support queues in the preceding example. Use a component that limits its output to the allowed answers and gives you a signal for when to escalate. Confident answers proceed, and uncertain ones escalate. The AWS Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens describes this tiered, confidence-based escalation . On AWS, you can build it four ways: A small Amazon Bedrock model with structured outputs – The answer is limited to an enum of options, plus an ‘unsure’ option that triggers escalation. This is the model’s own judgment, not a calibrated score, so check it against labeled data before you use it to decide escalation. Embedding similarity – Embed the input with an Amazon Bedrock embeddings model and pick the nearest labeled example. Use the similarity score as an escalation signal, and set its threshold on labeled data. Strands Decider , an experime

items.title: Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing
items.description: Today, Amazon SageMaker AI introduces KV cache-aware routing (KV-aware routing), a new routing strategy for real-time endpoints. It uses the cache state that the model container reports. It sends each request to an instance that already holds a long cached match for its prompt and isn’t too busy. It’s for teams that serve large language models (LLMs) with multi-turn conversations, long shared prompts, or heavy load. You turn it on in two places: add one environment variable to your model so the container reports its cache contents, and set RoutingStrategy to KV_AWARE in the endpoint configuration. Your clients call the endpoint with the same APIs as before. Here’s the problem it solves: LLM applications such as chat assistants, Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), and agents with long system prompts send many requests that start with the same text. A model keeps the work it did on a prompt in GPU memory, the KV cache, and skips that work when the same start reaches the same instance again. In part 1 of this series , we introduced prefix-aware routing for Amazon SageMaker AI, which sends requests that start the same way to the same instance. Prefix-aware routing infers where a prefix is cached from the request alone, so it can’t tell when an instance has evicted that cache. Prefix-aware routing picks an instance from the request alone. It hashes the start of the request, up to the PrefixLength you configure (bytes of the InvokeEndpoint payload, or characters of the message text for the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API), and sends requests that start the same way to the same instance. It never sees what an instance actually has cached. This works well when every request starts with the same shared text, and less well in two cases: The cache on an instance changes over time. An instance evicts older KV cache entries when its GPU memory fills up, but the router keeps sending matching requests there as if the cache were still warm. A conversation starts out short. In a multi-turn chat, each turn adds to the history. While the request is still shorter than PrefixLength , every new turn changes the text the router hashes, so the next turn can land on a different instance than the one that cached the earlier turns. The turns of a conversation stay on one instance only after the request grows past PrefixLength . In this post, we explain how KV-aware routing works, when to use it, and how to enable, invoke, and verify it on single model endpoints and inference component endpoints. How KV-aware routing works KV-aware routing has three parts: the model container reports what it has cached, SageMaker AI keeps a managed cache index of that state for the endpoint, and the endpoint uses the index to choose an instance for each request. When you turn events on with SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG , the container publishes a KV cache event each time it stores or evicts cache entries, and SageMaker AI uses these events to keep the index current. The index holds only pointers: one-way, truncated hashes of cached content, each mapped to the instance or inference component copy that holds it. It never stores prompts, token IDs, request payloads, or KV tensors. When a request arrives, the endpoint tokenizes the prompt and looks up the tokens in the index. The index returns the instances or inference component copies that hold part of the prompt in their cache, and how much of it each one holds. For example, if instance A holds the cached start of a conversation, the next turn of that conversation goes to A. Because the index matches on tokens rather than a fixed number of bytes, a multi-turn history can match in full as it grows. A request that shares only part of its prompt still goes to the instance with the longest match. The endpoint then picks among these candidates by weighing how much of the prompt each one has cached against how busy it is. A candidate that is too busy is skipped, so if the instance with the longest match is busy, the request goes to the next-best one that is available. If no candidate has a useful match or all of them are busy, the request falls back to load-aware routing, as described in Routing overhead and fallbacks. You don’t configure a concurrency threshold for this, as you do with prefix-aware routing. The index also follows the fleet. When you scale in, entries for removed instances are dropped. When you scale out or an update replaces instances, the new instances start with empty caches, so latency can be higher for a short time. Figure 1: KV-aware routing on a SageMaker AI endpoint. The router looks up the managed cache index and forwards the request to the instance that holds the longest cached match. Each instance reports KV cache events back to the index In Figure 1, the endpoint has three instances, A, B, and C. Each instance runs the same model in its own model container (the AWS vLLM Deep Learning Container listed in Requirements and limits) and has its own KV cache in GPU memory, so each instance holds different cached content: A holds turns 1 to 3 of conversation 1, B holds conversations 2 and 3, and C holds document 7. When turn 4 of conversation 1 arrives (step 1), the router tokenizes it and looks it up in the managed cache index (step 2). The index shows that A holds the first 6,000 of the request’s 6,200 tokens, so the router sends the request to A (step 3), and A only has to compute the remaining tokens. If A is busy, the router sends the request to the least busy instance instead (step 4). KV-aware routing needs a choice of destinations, so it is active only with at least two instances, or at least two copies of an inference component. With a single instance, every request goes to that instance and the setting has no effect. You set the strategy per production variant in the RoutingConfig of your endpoint configuration. Strategy How it rout

items.title: Govern and discover records with common metadata in AWS Agent Registry
items.description: As organizations build more agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and skills, they need a consistent way to describe, govern, and find them. AWS Agent Registry provides a catalog for registering, approving, and discovering these resources and custom records. Each record carries a name, a description, a protocol descriptor, and an approval status. However, every organization has attributes and facts that it wants to track, and some are unique to that organization, such as its business units, resource owners, risk classifications, and development environments. Organizations want one common definition for each of these attributes, and they want every agent, MCP server, and skill in the registry to carry these facts. Until now, organizations had no way to define these facts in AWS Agent Registry and store them on each record. Custom metadata schemas are now available in AWS Agent Registry. A custom metadata schema is a set of organization-defined key-value pairs that records in an AWS Agent Registry carry. An administrator defines the schema and applies it to the registry, and all records within the registry must then adhere to the schema. When publishers create or submit records, they supply values for the fields specified in the applicable schema, and AWS Agent Registry validates those values against the schema set by the admin. Approvers can rely on the validated values when reviewing a record, and consumers and agents can use them to discover and filter records. Administrators, publishers, security and governance teams, approvers, consumers, and agents all work from a shared set of facts to govern, discover, and understand the resources in their agentic fleet. In this post, we follow the AnyCompany organization publishing an MCP server with custom schema definition, enriching that record, and making it available for discovery by humans or agents. We use an MCP server as the example, but the same steps apply to other record types. How custom metadata works With custom metadata, an organization can use standardized vocabulary for describing its resources. The registry administrator defines the custom metadata schema : field names, types, allowed values, and whether each field is required or optional. The registry enforces the schema on every record, so a field such as environment has the same name and the same allowed values whichever team publishes the record. The schema has common attributes that apply to every record type, and you can add dedicated fields that only apply to specific record types. Each field is Text, Enum, URL, or Boolean. When a record is created or updated, the registry validates the custom metadata against the schema set up by the admin. If a record is created without any custom metadata, AWS Agent Registry saves it as NON_COMPLIANT . A team can save work in progress this way, but it can’t submit the record for approval until it has the required fields and values. If a record includes custom metadata with an unknown field, a missing required field, or an invalid value, AWS Agent Registry rejects it with a ValidationException . GetRegistryRecord returns the record’s custom metadata values and its compliance status. ( COMPLIANT means that the values match the administrator’s schema. It is not an approval. The approvers make that decision.) Discovery APIs also allow filtering records based on custom attributes. What custom metadata makes possible Because teams can describe the AWS Agent Registry records with the same fields and values, the registry can support and scale governance and compliance. Ownership and operations Fields such as environment ( prod , staging , or dev ), businessUnit , ownerTeam , supportContact , and costCenter record where a resource runs, who is responsible for it, and who pays for it. A configuration management database (CMDB) ID links the record to your existing inventory, and a support-tier field sets expectations for anyone who depends on the resource. Security and compliance Data classification, compliance scope such as Payment Card Industry (PCI) or Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), risk tier, scan status, and a scan report URL turn an approval into a check of structured evidence. Your existing scanners, CMDB sync jobs, and classification tools write these values through the API before a record is submitted. You can build your record approval process or automation using these values, as this post shows. Better discovery Custom metadata values are indexed for search. A consumer or agent can combine a natural-language query with specific metadata filters, such as environment=prod AND businessUnit=payments AND securityScanStatus=PASSED . Only approved records are returned, so a record that matches the filters but hasn’t been approved stays out of the results. Figure 1 shows how each role, from administrator to consumer, moves a record through schema definition, registration, enrichment, approval, and discovery. Figure 1: Swimlane diagram showing how a record moves through AWS Agent Registry, by role Walkthrough of an MCP record from registration to discovery AnyCompany operates anycompany-governed-registry , an AWS Agent Registry without auto-approval. Its payments team publishes an MCP record, payments-ledger-mcp , a read-only server for ledger lookups. Existing security and inventory systems enrich this MCP record before an approval function decides whether consumers can discover it. The five numbered steps in Figure 2 match the walkthrough: define, register, enrich and submit, review, then discover. Figure 2: Custom metadata gathers publisher context and values from your existing tools, so approval and search can use the same facts Prerequisites To follow the walkthrough, you need: An AWS account in a supported AWS Region . items.title: Secure OAuth patterns for Snowflake Cortex AI through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.description: Enterprises today need a clear way to extend their authentication and authorization controls into the agentic layer, often requiring either broad service account permissions or custom-built auth integrations that add operational overhead. When an AI agent running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model) needs to call the Snowflake-managed MCP server (which exposes Snowflake Cortex Agents as one of its tool types) through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the first question enterprises must answer is: how does the agent authenticate? In this post, we walk through three Open Authorization (OAuth) configurations we tested on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: Snowflake OAuth (per-user, no external Identity Provider, or IdP), three-legged OAuth with a third-party Identity Provider (corporate single sign-on, or SSO), and two-legged OAuth with a third-party Identity Provider (shared service user). Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity also supports an on-behalf-of (OBO) grant (TOKEN_EXCHANGE) that delivers per-user identity for unattended workloads without a consent prompt. We focus on the three configurations we tested end-to-end, flagging where OBO fits as we go. By the end, you will be able to identify which pattern suits your enterprise scenario. Solution overview Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, connects AI agents to external tool providers through MCP server targets. It targets the Snowflake-managed MCP server, which surfaces Cortex Search and Cortex Analyst as MCP tools that an MCP-aware client can discover and invoke. Rather than acting as a wrapper, the Gateway aggregates the capabilities of its configured targets into a single unified catalog, which it presents to the agent as one tools/list response. The core focus of this post is the outbound authentication for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway: how it obtains and presents OAuth tokens to the Snowflake-managed MCP server. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity acts as the credential broker: the Gateway obtains a workload token by calling GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT (because the Gateway uses JSON Web Token (JWT) inbound authentication), then calls GetResourceOauth2Token against the configured provider. AgentCore Identity owns the token vault, the token refresh, and the user-to-token binding, and it fetches, caches, and refreshes tokens automatically. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity supports three OAuth configurations spanning two grant types (authorization_code and client_credentials): Snowflake OAuth : Snowflake acts as its own OAuth authorization server. Each user authenticates directly to Snowflake through the Authorization Code grant (3LO). No external identity provider is needed. Three-legged OAuth using a third-party Identity Provider: Users authenticate through corporate SSO with the Authorization Code grant. Snowflake trusts IdP-issued JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) through its External OAuth security integration. Two-legged OAuth pattern using a third-party IdP: A shared service user authenticates through the client_credentials grant of the IdP. No user interaction or consent is required, which is ideal for machine-to-machine workloads. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity also offers an API-key credential provider (which supports Snowflake Programmatic Access Tokens). We focus on OAuth here for per-user attribution and automatic token refresh. Each configuration uses a credential provider in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity (CustomOauth2, OktaOauth2, or MicrosoftOauth2) and a corresponding security integration on the Snowflake side. Note: We tested these patterns with the Snowflake-managed MCP server using Okta and Microsoft Entra ID. Patterns 2 and 3 (external IdP) follow standard OAuth flows, so they can extend to other OAuth-protected MCP servers, but validate the token claims, scopes, and audience settings for your SaaS provider. Only Pattern 1 is Snowflake-specific, because it relies on Snowflake’s built-in OAuth authorization server. The Snowflake-specific elements are the OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER issuer-lock parameter, the session:role: / session:scope: grammar, BLOCKED_ROLES_LIST, LOGIN_NAME / EMAIL_ADDRESS mapping, and QUERY_HISTORY attribution. If your SaaS exposes its own internal OAuth server, you configure outbound OAuth the same way as Snowflake OAuth. Pattern OAuth grant AgentCore Identity credential provider vendor Snowflake security integration Snowflake query identity mapping Snowflake OAuth – 3LO authorization_code Custom provider (CustomOauth2) TYPE = OAUTH, OAUTH_CLIENT = CUSTOM The real user, with their assigned role 3LO with external IdP authorization_code Built-in provider (such as OktaOauth2, MicrosoftOauth2) TYPE = EXTERNAL_OAUTH + OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER (set with ALTER ACCOUNT / DATABASE / SCHEMA); EXTERNAL_OAUTH_TYPE = OKTA / AZURE / PING_FEDERATE / CUSTOM The real user, with their assigned role 2LO with external IdP client_credentials Built-in provider (such as OktaOauth2, MicrosoftOauth2) or CustomOauth2 TYPE = EXTERNAL_OAUTH + OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER (set with ALTER ACCOUNT / DATABASE / SCHEMA); EXTERNAL_OAUTH_TYPE = OKTA / AZURE / PING_FEDERATE / CUSTOM A shared Snowflake service user Notes: 2LO does not require a built-in vendor. CustomOauth2 with the CLIENT_CREDENTIALS grant can work with your choice of OAuth 2.0 authorization server. When Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway brokers the token (the pattern in this post), Snowflake validates it through the TYPE = EXTERNAL_OAUTH security integration. Setting OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER (with ALTER ACCOUNT, DATABASE, or SCHEMA) is what lets direct MCP clients auto-discover your IdP through the Protected Resource Metadata endpoint, and it issuer-locks the MCP endpoint to that integration. items.title: Announcing AI data preparation capabilities in Amazon SageMaker: Build high-quality datasets for model development workflows
items.description: Teams that ship generative AI to production know that a model is only as good as its data. That is why preparing high-quality training and evaluation data comes first. Fine-tuning an open-weight model, running reinforcement learning, or building an evaluation suite all depend on data that is accurate, well-labeled, and representative of your task. For narrow, well-defined tasks, a smaller model customized on clean, task-specific data can often match or exceed the accuracy of a larger general-purpose model prompted into shape, at a lower cost per inference. In practice, though, preparing that data is often the slowest part of the project. Labeled examples are scarce or expensive, and privacy rules limit what you can use. Quality problems such as duplicates, label noise, and answer leakage go unnoticed until a training run disappoints, and every training technique expects data in its own format. As a result, data scientists spend weeks wrangling data instead of building models. Today, we’re expanding Amazon SageMaker AI with new AI data preparation capabilities for model development workflows. You can generate synthetic examples, assess and improve existing datasets, and bring expert feedback into the process through Python SDK APIs and the AWS AI-ML agent skill. You work in your notebook or IDE, with specifications and code that you can inspect and change. Prepare data without hand-building pipelines With AI Data Preparation capabilities, you don’t need to stitch together labeling tools, generation scripts, and validation jobs. Each capability is a standalone building block. You can use one of them on its own or chain them together according to the workflow you want. Auto-labeling: Label data at scale from an unlabeled dataset, a small labeled seed set, or no labels at all. Built-in task types include classification, named entity recognition, extractive question answering, ordinal rating, and summarization, and you can define custom tasks. You describe the task in a short labeling spec, which is validated against your own examples before the full dataset is labeled. For tasks with a fixed set of possible answers, such as classification, named entity recognition, and extractive question answering, a jury of several models labels each row, and their level of agreement becomes that row’s confidence score. Human review: Rows below your confidence threshold go to a review queue in Amazon SageMaker Studio, which uses the open-source Label Studio Community Edition. Outside subject matter experts can access the review app through the link in the partner app box in SageMaker Studio. Reviewer corrections feed back into auto-labeling, and you can generate consensus metrics and labeling reports. Synthetic data generation: Generate training, evaluation, and test data from a specification. You can ground the output in your own seed data and documents, and the service generates a code-based data generation pipeline that you can review, modify, reuse, and scale. Data quality evaluation: Check datasets against your own business rules, built-in metrics, and LLM-as-a-judge metrics. Find duplicates and near-duplicates, and surface issues you didn’t think to check for, such as label noise or answer leakage. Data transformation: Clean and reshape data for your target training technique. Describe the change in plain language and have the code generated for you, use built-in operations such as dedupe, merge, split, and filter, or run your own Python at scale. You work wherever you already work. Use the SageMaker Python SDK directly or provide your coding agent the AI-ML skill in the agent toolkit and let your agent invoke the APIs according to established data science best practices. Describe what you need, and the agent selects and runs the right capability in SageMaker Studio JupyterLab, Kiro, or your local IDE with your coding assistant of choice. For teams building specialized models, the hardest part is often finding enough task-specific data. Splunk, a Cisco company, faced exactly this when building evaluation models for its Agent Observability product. “For Splunk Agent Observability, our ability to train robust GenAI Eval models relies on access to high-quality, diverse datasets which are hard to curate for very specific tasks. Amazon SageMaker AI data preparation capabilities for synthetic data generation is meaningfully helping us scale these capabilities. We’ve been able to generate statistically representative synthetic datasets reliably and fast, while preserving the underlying patterns our models depend on. The seamless integration with the rest of our SageMaker workflow means our data scientists and customers spend less time wrangling data and more time building models that drive real enterprise value through Splunk.” — Yash Sheth, Director of Engineering, Splunk Agent Observability Chain capabilities from raw data to training The value grows when you combine the capabilities. Some common patterns: Build a golden evaluation dataset: Auto-label your raw data from a small seed set. High-confidence rows are accepted automatically, and low-confidence rows go to human reviewers. Their corrections improve the next labeling pass, resulting in a trusted, human-validated dataset to benchmark your models against. Go from raw documents to a trained model in one workflow: Generate data: Synthetic data generation creates task-specific examples grounded in your documents and seed data. Transform it: Data transformation reshapes the data into the format your training technique expects, such as supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), or reinforcement learning (RL). Validate it: Data quality evaluation checks the dataset for duplicates, leakage, and rule violations before you spend compute on training. Train: Train with SageMaker AI model customization.
